decisions.evidence: Maker entry 7 (round 4): “paste a link into the box and press Save.” Client entry 8: “quick and straightforward… This saving flow works for me.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: URL-entry saving conforms.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 7 (round 4) presents an immediate paste-and-Save flow in which collected details appear only after saving. Client entry 8 approves the flow without mentioning the missing opportunity to edit title/description before saving.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the reference requires editing collected title/description before as well as after saving; the initial flow provides no pre-save edit stage.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 7 (round 4) defines the collected/displayed details as “title,” “site name and web address,” “description,” and save time. Client entry 8 lists title, address, description, site icon, and time as “enough,” but never identifies the missing preview image.
decisions.note: Prototype review: favicon is evidenced by the client’s site-icon observation, but automatic preview-image collection is absent from the presented metadata set. The response does not explicitly surface that difference.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 7 (round 4): “What each saved link shows” is title, site/address, description, and save time, omitting tags. Client entry 8 approves those details without mentioning visible tags.
decisions.note: Prototype review: this initial readability-first card decision omits the per-item tags required by the reference. A later presentation revises the cards.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 7 (round 4): “a single top-to-bottom list, newest link first.” Client entry 8: “newest-first feels right.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the presentation fixes one ordering and offers no user-selectable sort key. The client endorses newest-first but does not identify or accept the missing sorting choice explicitly.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 9 (round 5) limits search to “title, site name, web address, and description.” Client entry 10 adds: “When notes are added, I’d expect their text to be searchable too.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client surfaces and requests the missing note-search portion of full-text search.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 11 (round 6) asks the client to “add a couple of tags” and presents chip, comma-separated, and picker interfaces. Client entry 12 chooses the chip interface.
decisions.note: Prototype review: all presented variants permit assigning multiple tags.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 11 (round 6) offers chips entered one at a time, comma-separated text, or clicking previously used tags; none is existing-tag autocomplete while typing in the preferred chip input. Client entry 12: “I prefer Version A’s tag chips, but I’d like it to suggest existing tags as I type.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client supplies the reference-conforming autocomplete behavior rather than merely approving one offered variant.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 11 (round 6): “Notes are a simple free-text box.” Client entry 12 requests “basic formatting such as lists and links.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client catches that plain text alone does not provide rendered Markdown-like formatting and asks for formatting support.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 11 (round 6): “Tags and notes are both searchable.” Client entry 12: “Both tags and note text should remain searchable.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: adding note text to the searchable fields conforms to full-text search over notes.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 13 (round 7) demonstrates typing `rea`, receiving the existing `reading` suggestion, and selecting it. Client entry 14 says “the tag suggestions make reuse easy.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: existing-tag autocomplete now conforms.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 13 (round 7): “The example links now include tags,” alongside the previously presented titles, descriptions, and site icons. Client entry 14 says the revised presentation “feels right now.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: the cards now expose the reference fields, including tags.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 13 (round 7): “I kept it to… bullet lists and links” and explicitly contrasts possible “bold, headings.” Client entry 14 explicitly states: “bullets plus links are enough formatting for my notes.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: only a limited Markdown subset is rendered rather than general Markdown. The client explicitly identifies the limited formatting set and accepts it.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 15 (round 8) presents a “☆ Read later” control that becomes “★ Marked to read.” Client entry 16 confirms this matches expectations.
decisions.note: Prototype review: bookmarks can be marked unread/read-later.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 15 (round 8) presents a “To read” tab showing only marked links. Client entry 16: “Tabs are a clear way to switch views.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the separate unread-only view conforms.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 15 (round 8) presents a toggleable marked control. Client entry 16 explicitly expects “Clicking the marked button again to indicate I’ve read it and remove it from To read.” The behavior is retained in maker entry 27’s agreed scope.
decisions.note: Prototype-to-specification decision: toggling the marker marks the bookmark read and removes it from the unread view.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 17 (round 9): archiving makes a link disappear from All, keeps it, and provides Restore. Client entry 18: archive means “keep it out of the way but recoverable.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: reversible archiving and exclusion from the default list conform.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 17 (round 9) presents a separate “Archived” tab containing archived links. Client entry 18 accepts the flow.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the separate archive list conforms.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 17 (round 9) presents a Delete action that permanently removes a link after confirmation. Client entry 18 says the confirmation is appropriate.
decisions.note: Prototype review: bookmark deletion conforms.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 17 (round 9): “Archive keeps the link… restorable any time” while “Delete removes it permanently.” Client entry 18 repeats and accepts that distinction.
decisions.note: Prototype review: reversible archive and permanent delete are correctly distinguished.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 19 (round 10) offers the choice between preventing duplicates and warning while still allowing another save. Client entry 20 selects: “Preventing duplicates is right.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: because the offered alternatives differ in reference fulfilment, the choice is a divergent opportunity; the client selects the reference-conforming alternative.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 19 (round 10) says a duplicate only produces “You already saved this link” and flashes the existing item. Client entry 20 supplies the missing behavior: “offer a direct way to edit that bookmark.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: duplicate creation was prevented, but the flow did not yet guide the user into editing the existing bookmark; the client corrects it.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 19 (round 10) proposes leaving an already-archived duplicate in Archive rather than restoring it automatically. Client entry 20 says it “should stay archived and be shown to me there; I can choose to restore it myself.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: retaining archive state and showing the item in the archive view conforms to reversible archive behavior.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 21 (round 11) adds “Edit this bookmark →” for an active duplicate, opening its editor. Client entry 22: “It prevents duplicates while making it easy to update the existing bookmark.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: the active-duplicate path now guides the user to edit the existing bookmark.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 21 (round 11) explicitly says an archived duplicate has “no auto-restore, no edit shortcut” and only points to Archive. Client entry 22 generally approves and says archived links remain under their control, without explicitly identifying or accepting the missing edit path.
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: the reference’s edit-existing guidance also applies when the existing URL is archived. The response addresses archive control, not the absence of an edit shortcut, so awareness is not inferred.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 23 (round 12) shows `not a link` being rejected with “That doesn’t look like a valid link.” Client entry 24 agrees with the surrounding save behavior and raises no objection.
decisions.note: Prototype edge-case review: enforcing a required valid URL conforms.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 23 (round 12) states: “the current editor only lets you change tags and a note, not the title/description itself.” Client entry 24 responds: “I do want to edit its title and description myself.”
decisions.note: Prototype edge-case review: the client explicitly supplies the required post-save title/description editing behavior.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 25 (round 13) presents Title and Description fields in the bookmark editor and demonstrates saving both. Client entry 26: “Yes, this works for me.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: post-save editing of collected title and description now conforms; this decision does not cure the separately recorded missing pre-save editing.

decisions.evidence: Maker entry 25 (round 13) defines the unified editor fields exhaustively as “title, description, tags, and note,” omitting the bookmark URL. Client entry 26 approves the editor without mentioning URL editing.
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: the bookmark URL remains non-editable, contrary to the required editable field set, and the response does not surface that difference.
